title: What time is it? — and one famous trap
goal: Tell the time, name the days, and make plans. Along the way, meet one famous trap: Russian "half nine" doesn't mean what a Brit would think.
bekal: name the days of the week and say "on …day"
name the parts of the day: morning, afternoon, evening, night

dialogs.title: Диалог — Making plans
dialogs.intro: Ani and Марко arrange a study session by text, then meet in person. Watch line nine: the Russian way of saying "half past" counts toward the next hour.

lines.speaker: Марко:
lines.literal: hi! when — at — you — free — time?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.literal: on — Wednesday — and — on — Friday. and — what?

lines.speaker: Марко:
lines.id: Let's study together. Is Wednesday OK?
lines.literal: let's — study — together. on — Wednesday — normal?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: I have a class at three. Let's say five.
lines.literal: at — three — at — me — lesson. let's — at — five.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: At the library. It's open until nine.
lines.literal: in — library. it — works — until — nine.

lines.speaker: Марко:
lines.id: Great. By the way, what time is it now?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Half past eight. Poldevyatovo, for short.

lines.speaker: Марко:
lines.id: "Half of the ninth" — so that's eight thirty?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Yes! It's exactly the same in Indonesian. Finally something easy!
lines.literal: yes! in — Indonesian — language — exactly — so — same. finally — something — easy!

notes: **This is the big trap: Russian "half" points to the *next* hour.** *Половина девятого* literally means "half of the ninth (hour)" = **8:30**. ⚠️ English speakers stumble badly here, because British *half nine* means 9:30. Think "halfway into the ninth hour," and you'll get it right. (Ani is pleased because Indonesian, German, and Dutch count the same way as Russian.)
**The short form is written as one word: полдевятого, полшестого, полодиннадцатого.** That's what people actually say in conversation. The long form *половина девятого* sounds a bit more formal.

**Час / часа / часов follow the number rule from Unit 7.** 1 час, 2–4 часа, 5+ часов. So: *час* (one o'clock), *два часа* (two o'clock), *пять часов* (five o'clock), *двенадцать часов* (twelve o'clock). ⚠️ Note that one o'clock does **not** use один: just *час*.

**To say when something happens, use в + the number.** *В три часа* (at three), *в пять* (at five), *в час* (at one). Before some hard-to-say consonant clusters, в becomes **во**: *во сколько?* (at what time?), *во вторник* (on Tuesday).

**Days of the week take в + accusative.** *в понедельник*, *в среду*, *в пятницу*. Note среда → сред**у** and пятница → пятниц**у** — the feminine accusative ending from Unit 8. Days ending in a consonant (понедельник, вторник, четверг) don't change.
**До means "until" and takes the genitive.** *до девяти* (until nine), *до субботы* (until Saturday), *до свидания* (until the meeting — now you know why свидание became свидания).
**Кстати means "by the way," and Russians use it all the time.** It's the smoothest way to change the subject.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: There are two ways: the official way (like train timetables) and the everyday way.

after: ⚠️ The 3:15 and 4:45 forms use ordinal numbers (четвёртого = "of the fourth") and aren't required at A1. When in doubt, use the official way, which is always correct: **три пятнадцать** (3:15), **четыре сорок пять** (4:45). Russians use it too, especially for timetables.
Russian uses the 24-hour clock in writing (18:00) but the 12-hour clock in speech, with a tag: *шесть часов **вечера*** (six in the evening), *шесть часов **утра*** (six in the morning).

grammars.title: Days and parts of the day
body: Days take **в + accusative**; parts of the day use instrumental forms you simply memorize.
after: ⚠️ Russian divides the day a little differently from English. **День** runs roughly from 12 to 5 p.m., **вечер** from 5 p.m. until bedtime, and **ночь** is when people are asleep — roughly midnight to dawn. So *спокойной ночи* (good night) is said when parting for bed, not when meeting someone at 8 p.m. To greet someone at 8 p.m., say **добрый вечер**.
**Сегодня** today, **завтра** tomorrow, **вчера** yesterday, **послезавтра** the day after tomorrow, **позавчера** the day before yesterday.

blocks.title: Занят, свободен — short adjectives that follow gender
items: ⚠️ A woman says **Я занята** (*za-ni-TA*), a man says **Я занят** (*ZA-nit*). The ending changes and the stress moves. The same goes for **свободен / свободна**, **готов / готова** (ready), **должен / должна** (must).
These are short adjectives — forms used only after the subject, never in front of a noun. You don't need to master them now; learn the four pairs above as chunks.
**Договорились** literally means "we have agreed" — a very Russian way to wrap up making plans. It's like "OK, deal."
